title: Pricing Services
summary: Build your rate → Pick a pricing method → Quote it honestly → Raise it without drama
subtitle: Charge a price that pays your costs, your time, and your future.

blocks.text: Pricing a service is harder than pricing a product, because your main ingredient is your own time. Many new owners guess at a number that feels polite, then wonder why they are worn out and still behind on bills. This lesson shows you how to build a price from real numbers and quote it honestly under Canadian rules.

items.title: BUSINESS COSTS
items.text: Tools, software, insurance, phone, travel and ads. If the price doesn’t cover them, you pay them out of your own pocket.

items.title: YOUR PAY
items.text: The income you started the business for, before income tax and CPP come out of it.

items.title: TIME NOBODY PAYS FOR
items.text: Quotes, emails, driving, buying parts and cleaning up. It is real work, so the paid hours must carry it.

blocks.text: Beginners often copy a competitor’s price or reuse the hourly wage from their old job. Neither one pays for the costs of running a business, your own taxes or the unpaid hours around every paid hour.

items.title: “Being the cheapest is the safest way to win clients.”
items.text: A rock-bottom price draws customers who care only about price, and it leaves you no room for mistakes. Many buyers also read a price that low as a sign of weak quality.

blocks.text: Stop guessing, and build a price you can defend.
blocks.detail: A short calculation shows the hourly rate your business needs, so you can quote with confidence instead of worry.
blocks.extra: Section 02 builds that rate from real numbers.

sections.title: Build Your Rate From Real Numbers

blocks.text: Start with the pay you want before tax, and add your yearly business costs. Then divide by the hours you can bill in a year. Here is one handyman’s year, line by line.
$60,000 pay + $9,000 costs = $69,000 a year. Divided by 1,000 billable hours, that is $69 an hour.
blocks.extra: If you could bill 1,500 hours, the same year would need only $46 an hour. Few solo owners manage that many.

items.text: Before income tax and CPP. Is it enough to live on?

blocks.text: Where 1,000 billable hours come from

items.title: Weeks you work
items.text: 46 — after six weeks of holidays, sick days and slow weeks that nobody pays for.

items.title: Hours you work
items.text: About 1,840 — 40 hours a week for 46 weeks.

items.title: Hours nobody pays for
items.text: About 840 — quotes, travel, buying parts, messages and books.

items.title: Hours you can bill
items.text: About 1,000 — roughly 22 a week, or a little over half your working time.

blocks.text: Count the time off you won’t be paid for. No one pays a self-employed person for holidays or sick days. If you take six weeks off a year and bill about 22 hours in each of the other 46 weeks, that is roughly 1,000 billable hours. Your $60,000 is also before tax: as a sole proprietor you pay income tax and both halves of CPP out of it.

items.title: Measure the job before you name the price.
items.text: Measure the job before you name the price.

blocks.text: On $60,000 of net self-employment income, CPP alone is about $6,700: 11.9% of earnings above $3,500. Part of it comes back as a deduction and a tax credit, but you still pay it up front. Quebec residents pay QPP instead. Income tax comes on top, so set aside a share of every payment from day one.

items.title: “My old hourly wage is a fair rate for my business.”
items.text: An employer paid for your tools, your benefits, half your CPP and your paid holidays. As a business owner you pay all of that yourself, so your rate has to be well above your old wage.

sections.title: Pick the Pricing Method That Fits the Job

blocks.text: The hourly rate is your floor, not always the way you should charge. Choose the method that matches how the client thinks about the work.

items.title: Hourly rate
list: How it works: Your rate multiplied by the hours that a job takes
Best for: Work where the time is hard to predict

items.title: Fixed price
list: How it works: One price for a clearly described job
Best for: Work that you can scope in advance

items.title: Packages or value pricing
list: How it works: A set price based on the result for the customer
Best for: Work where the result matters more than the hours

blocks.text: One bathroom fan, priced three ways

items.title: Hourly
items.text: $187.50 — 2.5 hours at $69, plus the $15 call-out. The client carries the risk if the job runs long.

items.title: Fixed price
items.text: $210 — you carry the risk, and you keep the gain if you finish in two hours.

items.title: Package
items.text: $390 — fan, smoke-alarm check and fresh caulking, priced on the result: a quiet, dry bathroom.

items.title: Parts
items.text: Extra — list the fan and materials on their own line, so the client sees what they paid for.

blocks.text: Fixed prices reward your speed. When you quote a fixed price, you keep the gain as you get faster. Describe the job in writing first, including what is not included, so a small job does not slowly grow into a much bigger one.
Three add-ons worth setting now

items.title: MINIMUM CHARGE
items.text: Set the smallest job you will take, such as two hours. A 20-minute fix across town can cost more in travel than it earns.

items.title: CALL-OUT OR TRAVEL FEE
items.text: Cover driving and setup time. If every client must pay it, include it in the price you advertise.

items.title: RUSH OR AFTER-HOURS RATE
items.text: Charge more for evenings, weekends or next-day work. It protects your time and rewards clients who plan ahead.

blocks.text: The Competition Act bans price claims that mislead in a way that matters. Since June 23, 2022, advertising a price that leaves out a fixed fee everyone must pay counts as misleading. This is called drip pricing. The only exception is a charge the government sets, such as sales tax.
What every written quote includes

items.title: What the job includes
items.text: And, just as important, what it doesn’t.

items.title: The total price
items.text: With every required fee already in it.

items.title: Sales tax on its own line
items.text: If you are registered, so a $1,000 job in Ontario shows $130 HST, not a surprise $1,130.

items.title: Payment terms and deposit
items.text: Ask for a deposit on larger jobs, so you aren’t paying for materials out of your own pocket.

items.title: How long the quote is good for
items.text: For example, 30 days, because your costs change.

blocks.text: In Ontario, a supplier who gives a consumer a written estimate can’t charge more than 10% above it unless the client agrees to the new price. Other provinces have their own estimate rules, so treat every estimate as a promise and ask before the work grows.

The Red Toolbox
paragraphs: Hamid Rahimi was a handyman in Regina. He carried everything in a rusty red toolbox his uncle had given him. His goal was to quit his evening warehouse shift, which meant earning enough from repairs alone to cover his rent.
He charged $25 an hour, because that was what he earned at the warehouse. Clients loved him, and his calendar filled up within weeks. Yet at the end of the month, the numbers looked wrong.

Hamid sat at his kitchen table and added things up. He took off fuel, tools and insurance. Then he counted the hours he spent driving, quoting and answering messages. After costs, he was making about $9 an hour. He felt a flash of embarrassment, then a bigger flash of clarity.

Now he had a choice. He could keep the low price, keep every client and stay tired. Or he could work out a rate that would let him quit the warehouse, and risk losing some of them. He used the calculation from this lesson and landed on $55 an hour, plus a $15 call-out fee that he now built into every quote. He emailed his clients the new rates with a short, polite note.
He braced for the worst. Two of his eleven clients left. One of the others wrote back, “Finally. I was worried you couldn’t stay in business at that price.”

Within three months, Hamid worked fewer hours and earned more than before. He handed in his notice at the warehouse in the spring. The rusty red toolbox still rides in his truck, because he says it earned its place.

blocks.text: Hamid’s numbers, before and after

items.title: Old rate
items.text: $25 an hour — about $9 once fuel, tools, insurance and unpaid hours came out.

items.title: New rate
items.text: $55 an hour — plus a $15 call-out fee built into every quote.

items.title: Clients
items.text: 11 → 9 — two left, and one cheered.

items.title: Three months later
items.text: Fewer hours — more money, and notice handed in at the warehouse.

blocks.text: A fair price is a kindness to your clients and to yourself.
blocks.detail: When your price covers your real costs, you can do careful work, stay in business and keep serving the people who value you.
blocks.extra: Section 06 shows how Hamid told his clients, and how you can too.

blocks.text: Costs rise and your skills grow, so review your price every six months. A small, regular increase is easier on everyone than a big jump after years of standing still.
What a raise can survive

items.title: Before
items.text: $1,650 a week — 30 billable hours at $55.

items.title: After
items.text: 27.5 hours — all you need at $60 to earn the same $1,650.

items.title: Room to lose
items.text: About 8% — you could lose one client in twelve and still earn the same.

items.title: Most likely
items.text: More pay — most clients stay when the notice is fair and the work is good.

items.title: Recheck the formula
items.text: Update your pay goal, costs and billable hours.

items.title: Compare locally
items.text: Test the new rate against what similar businesses charge.

items.title: Give notice
items.text: Tell current clients at least a month ahead.

items.title: Thank loyal clients
items.text: Think about keeping a long-time client’s old rate for a few months.

blocks.text: A message you can adapt
“Thank you for trusting me with your repairs this year. Starting March 1, my rate will be $55 an hour, plus a $15 call-out fee that is included in every quote. I’m grateful to keep working with you.”
A fair price needs no apology. Keep the message short and warm, and give the date and the new rate.

items.title: “I should raise my price only when I lose my best clients.”
items.text: A small, regular increase is easier on everyone. Give clients notice, explain what changed, and think about keeping a loyal client’s old rate for a few months as a thank-you.

items.title: What three things must a service price cover?
items.detail: Your costs, your own pay, and the time you cannot bill.

items.title: Where does a mandatory $15 call-out fee belong?
items.text: since drip pricing is not allowed.

items.title: Can you add sales tax after the advertised price?
items.text: because government-imposed tax is the exception.

items.title: You want $60,000 before tax and have $9,000 of costs. About how much must you bill? A. $60,000 · B. $69,000 · C. $51,000
items.text: Your sales must cover both your pay and your business costs.

items.title: Which price is the safest to advertise? A. A price that leaves out a mandatory fee · B. The total price including all mandatory fixed fees, before tax · C. A price that changes at checkout
items.text: Mandatory fixed fees belong in the price. Government tax is the main exception.

items.title: Why does a written quote help? A. It protects both you and the client by recording the scope and price · B. It lets you change the price later · C. It is required for every job
items.text: A written quote prevents misunderstandings about the work and the cost.

items.title: You gave an Ontario client a written estimate of $800. The job now looks like $950. What should you do?
items.text: That is more than 10% over the estimate, so get the client’s agreement to the new price, in writing, before you go on.

items.title: You raise your rate from $55 to $60. About what share of your billable hours could you lose and still earn the same?
items.text: $55 ÷ $60 = 0.917, so 27.5 hours at $60 pays the same as 30 hours at $55.

items.title: In one sentence, say what you will change about the way you quote prices.
items.text: I will build my rate from my real costs and put every fee in the written quote.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Rate Card

blocks.text: Use rough yearly numbers. Round to the nearest hundred if that’s easier, and leave out bank and client details.
Your rate is a floor, not a ceiling. Quote above it when the job is urgent, risky or worth more to the client, and never quote below it to win a job you will resent.
Build your price from real numbers, include every mandatory fee, show tax separately, and put the quote in writing.

items.title: Billable hours
items.text: The hours you can charge a client for.

items.title: Overhead
items.text: The ongoing costs of running your business.

items.title: Fixed price
items.text: One agreed price for a clearly described job.

items.title: Value pricing
items.text: A price based on the result for the customer, not the hours.

items.title: Drip pricing
items.text: Advertising a price that leaves out fees everyone must pay.

items.title: Quote
items.text: A written price for a defined piece of work.

items.title: Estimate
items.text: A written guess at the price, which some provincial laws limit you to exceeding by a set amount.

quiz.question: You want $60,000 before tax and have $9,000 of costs. About how much must you bill?

questions: How much do you want to earn in a year before tax? A rough figure is fine.
What are your yearly business costs? Add tools, software, insurance, phone, travel and ads.
How many hours could you bill in a year, after time off and unpaid work?
What hourly rate does that give you, and what do similar local businesses charge?
Is there a required fee, such as a call-out or booking fee, that is not in your quoted price yet?
Which pricing method suits most of your jobs: hourly, fixed price or packages? Why?
